newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: 90 percent of women survive breast cancer - study.
newsitem.headline: 90 percent of women survive breast cancer - study.

text.p: Nine out of 10 women are still alive five years after breast cancer treatment, according to a new study presented by cancer experts on Monday.

Speaking at a conference on cancer in Vienna, Professor Harry Bartelink, Head of Radiation Oncology at Netherlands Cancer Institute, said the preliminary results of the study showed breast cancer treatment was achieving impressive survival rates.
The study, conducted in 35 countries, involved over 5,500 women who all received a combination of radiotherapy and conservative surgery for tumours up to five cm (two ins) in diameter.
"That we are able to prevent local recurrences in 92 percent of our patients after five years in so many countries in Europe, that is a breakthrough," he told Reuters.
But he warned it was unlikely the survival rate for women 10 years after treatment would ever be as good as for five years, because the disease often recurs after 15 to 20 years.
One European woman in 10 develops breast cancer.

Bartelink told delegates at the European Society of Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology conference that previous trials revealed similar survival rates, but those tests had such variations between centres that a new quality control programme had to be set up.
He said the overall survival rate had improved by 20 percent with the new study, and the control rate by 15 percent.
In the latest trial, the patients were divided into two groups, one receiving an extra radiotherapy boost dose and the other no additional dose.
He said in two years long-term patient follow-up should show whether the radiotherapy boost dose increased survival chances even more than the current 92 percent rate.
"In the meantime, it is clear the combination of radiotherapy and conservative surgery offers women effective treatment for breast cancer," he said.
The radiotherapy, given as a small daily dose over six weeks, produced virtually no side-effects, he added. The psychological burden of having the disease was the worst part.
"These results give hope to both patients and doctors," he said, but noted it was important to establish quality controls across Europe so the disease could be properly monitored.
In a separate study, experts found that smoking in lung cancer patients reduced the effect of radiation treatment.
"Cancer patients who are smokers should be told that giving up smoking can improve their chances of survival," said Dr Cai Grau at Denmark's Aarhus University Hospital Oncology Department.
Smokers had less oxygen in their blood, which was needed for a good response to radiotherapy, he said.
Another new study found small or single doses of radiotherapy provided effective relief for terminally ill cancer patients, with no severe adverse effects.

"Despite this, there are still many patients in Europe who are not being offered small doses of radiotherapy as part of their palliative care," said Jens Overgaard, Professor of Oncology at Aarhus University.
Radiotherapy was not being made available to patients simply because many health professionals were not aware of its benefits, but it was a good, low-cost treatment, he said.
